word_order: SOV — verbs/predicates consistently appear clause-finally, e.g. '식당 밥 먹다 보면은', '적성에 맞는지 안 맞는지부터 판단을 한 후에', with objects/complements preceding the verb throughout.
punctuation_present: sometimes — periods and question marks appear in some sentences (e.g. 4, 5, 13, 17) but many utterances end without any final punctuation (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 6, 9)
register: spontaneous conversational speech (transcribed casual dialogue/monologue, informal register with false starts and fillers)
non_boundary_traps: 뭐 (filler, not 'what' as a question word here)
그 (demonstrative filler, not a full noun phrase)
거 같애/같은데 (evidential hedge fused to prior clause, not a new sentence)
repeated words like '이거 이거 이거' (repetition/hesitation, not enumeration)
target_language_risks: Korean is pro-drop and topic-marked, so segments without prior context lose subject/object identity when rendered in English, which requires explicit subjects
Verb-final structure means the core meaning (verb, negation, tense, mood) is revealed only at clause end, so early segmentation risks mistranslating polarity or aspect
Sentence-final particles like -거든, -잖아, -같애 carry evidential/attitudinal nuance that has no single English equivalent and can be lost if segmented before the ending is seen
Fillers and false starts (뭐, 그, 이제) if segmented as separate units may be mistranslated as content words
Honorific/informal register markers affect tone in English (e.g. formal '-습니다' vs casual '-어/-야') and must be preserved consistently across segments
notes_for_prompt_writer: This is unscripted spoken Korean with frequent self-repair, fillers, and clause-chaining via connective endings (-는데, -고, -서, -니까) rather than explicit conjunctions; treat these endings as the primary segmentation cues since the verb (and thus polarity/tense) always comes last. Do not split on commas or fillers like 뭐/그/이제 alone, as these are hesitation markers, not clause boundaries. Because subjects and objects are frequently omitted (pro-drop) and topic particles are the main structural device, downstream segments longer than one clause may be needed to preserve referential clarity in the English output.
